stories.title: Dog abuse incident in southern China sparks protests
stories.summary: The brutal killing of a stray dog, Wang, and her puppies in Jieyang, Guangdong, sparked protests and calls for better animal welfare across over 100 Chinese cities. Videos of the abuse circulated online, leading to international awareness with adverts in Taipei, Tokyo, and New York, but Chinese authorities censored related social media posts. Activists faced police warnings, yet people in Hong Kong mourned Wang and urged that such animal cruelty tragedies must never happen again. The brutal killing of a stray dog and her puppies in China in June has ignited widespread condemnation, prompting animal lovers and activists to call for improved animal welfare, with protests even taking place abroad. Calls for better legal protection for animals have grown in more than 100 Chinese cities since the incident took place on June 28 in a village in Jieyang in the southern Chinese province of Guangdong. Adverts and videos in remembrance of the stray dog, known as Wang, subsequently appeared on large outdoor screens in Taipei, Tokyo and New York, with related protests planned to be held in Nagoya in Japan this November. Wang, who had subsisted on help from villagers in Jieyang, was repeatedly beaten and then set on fire by several boys under 14 years old, with her three puppies also killed, according to reports. The minors, whose motives were unclear, were sent to correctional facilities. The attention received by the incident also appeared to come to the notice of China’s censors, with related posts on Chinese social media platforms beginning to vanish. Jieyang authorities, meanwhile, appealed to the public not to spread information about it. Social media posts by some celebrities about the incident were later found to have disappeared, while some individuals were reportedly warned by the police and asked to stop their activism. In Hong Kong, mourners paid their respects to Wang after news about the abuse spread on social media.

stories.headline: Construction safety design needed to reduce fatal accidents in Hong Kong: experts

opening: Hong Kong should make safety design a part of all building development plans and address the culture of rushing work at construction sites, industry leaders have said after the city recorded 15 fatal industrial accidents earlier this year.

Their calls followed the warning by Construction Industry Council chairman Thomas Ho On-sing on Monday that the number of such accidents was on the rise despite stiffer penalties, reflecting that a safety culture had failed to take root.
